extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying introductory set theory / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, proof techniques, and exercise guidance for comparing cardinalities of sets (countable vs uncountable), proving bijections/injections/surjections, and using the Cantor and Cantor–Bernstein–Schroeder results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same cardinality (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: |A| = |B| if and only if there exists a bijection A^B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a bijection between the two sets to declare they have the same cardinality. (The text repeatedly uses this as the fundamental criterion for 'same size'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of cardinalities is an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality of cardinalities is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflexive: identity function A→A is a bijection so |A| = |A|. Symmetric: inverse of a bijection A→B is a bijection B→A so |A| = |B| implies |B| = |A|. Transitive: composition of bijections is a bijection, so |A| = |B| and |B| = |C| imply |A| = |C|. Use transitivity to prove equalities by finding an intermediate set B with known equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove equal cardinality by producing a bijection (formula not table)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show two given sets have equal cardinality, describe a bijection from one to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise instruction: 'Describe your bijection with a formula (not as a table).' When possible give an explicit formula for the bijection rather than only an ad-hoc listing or table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countably infinite (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A is countably infinite if |N| = |A|, that is, there exists a bijection N → A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, think of a bijection f:N→A as 'counting' the elements of A: f(1), f(2), f(3), ... . The cardinality of N is denoted Kq (aleph naught).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncountable (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A is uncountable if A is infinite and |N| ≠ |A| (i.e., there exists no bijection N → A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the absence of a bijection with N to declare uncountability. The text treats many examples by showing impossibility of listing elements as a count.

rubrics_metrics.name: List characterization of countability (Theorem 13.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is countably infinite iff its elements can be arranged in an infinite list a1,a2,a3,...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an explicit listing to prove countability; conversely, a listing defines a bijection f(n)=an from N to A. This characterization is used repeatedly (e.g., primes, even integers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove Q is countable by arranging in array and following diagonal path (Theorem 13.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove the rationals Q are countably infinite, arrange all rationals in an infinite array (columns by numerator in reduced form) and follow a snaking/infinite path that visits every rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reduced forms appear in the correct column (avoid non-reduced duplicates), then traverse the table along a specified path to produce an infinite list containing every rational number once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of countable sets is countable (Theorem 13.5 and Corollary 13.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are countably infinite, then A×B is countably infinite; by induction, finite Cartesian products of countable sets are countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct listings for A and B and use an infinite path (zig-zag through the grid) to list all ordered pairs. For n>2 use induction and pair grouping to reduce to the two-factor case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of two countable sets is countable (Theorem 13.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are countably infinite, then A∪B is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interleave (shuffle) the two lists: a1, b1, a2, b2, a3, b3, ... and avoid listing elements twice if they belong to both sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite subset of a countable set is countable (Theorem 13.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinite subset A of a countably infinite set B is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a listing of B, form a listing of A by traversing B's listing in order and selecting elements that belong to A; the resulting list is infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superset-of-uncountable implies uncountable (Theorem 13.9 / containment principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊆ A and X is uncountable, then A is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of an uncountable subset inside A forces A to be uncountable; this is often used to show a set is uncountable by embedding a known uncountable set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing cardinalities via injections and surjections (Definition 13.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) |A| = |B| means there is a bijection A→B. (2) |A| < |B| means there is an injection A→B but no surjection A→B. (3) |A| ≤ |B| means |A| < |B| or |A| = |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finite sets this matches intuitive counting. For infinite sets, demonstrate an injection to show ≤, and to show strict < show that no surjection exists (often via diagonal argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem for power set (Theorem 13.7)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit the injection f(x) = {x} from A into P(A). To show no surjection A → P(A) exists, use the diagonal (Cantor) argument: define B = {x ∈ A : x ∉ f(x)} and derive a contradiction from assuming a surjection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cantor diagonalization to show no surjection exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming there is no surjection from a set A onto another set (often P(A) or the reals), use diagonal-type subset constructions to obtain contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: assume surjection f, define a set B depending on membership in f(x), then argue B cannot be in the image of f (leads to contradiction). The text applies this in Theorem 13.7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor–Bernstein–Schroeder theorem (Theorem 13.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are injections f:A→B and g:B→A, then there exists a bijection h:A→B (hence |A| = |B|).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of finding a bijection directly, it suffices to find injections both ways. The standard constructive proof partitions A into G and W (gray and white) with G = ⋃_{k≥0} (g∘f)^k(A−g(B)), define h(x)=f(x) for x∈G and h(x)=g^{-1}(x) for x∈W, and verify injectivity and surjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove cardinality equalities by finding injections both ways and applying Cantor–Bernstein
rubrics_metrics.description: To show two sets have the same cardinality, it's often easier to construct injections in each direction and apply Cantor–Bernstein–Schroeder rather than to construct an explicit bijection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [0,1) and (0,1) — give simple injections [0,1)→(0,1) and (0,1)→[0,1) then apply CBS to conclude existence of bijection. The text explicitly recommends this method for tricky bijections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing injections between continuum and P(N) via decimal expansions (proof strategy for |R| = |P(N)|)
rubrics_metrics.description: Build injections f:[0,1)→P(N) and g:P(N)→[0,1) using decimal expansions and digit-position encodings, taking care to avoid decimal representations that terminate in an infinite string of 9s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: map 0.d1d2d3... (no trailing 9s) to the set {i : di = 1, or scaled powers of 10 as in the text's construction}, and map a subset X⊆N to the decimal with 1's at indices in X. Show both maps are injective and apply Cantor–Bernstein to conclude |[0,1)| = |P(N)|, hence |R| = |P(N)|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise/verifications guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises frequently require: prove sets are countable/uncountable, give explicit bijection formulas, verify bijections given in examples, or use earlier exercises/theorems as suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific prompts: 'Verify that the function f in Example 13.3 is a bijection.' 'Find a formula for the bijection f in Example 13.2.' 'Use Theorem 13.3 to produce listings.' Follow suggestion notes (e.g., 'use Exercise 18 of Section 12.2') when directed.
